overview: Keppel DC REIT, listed on the SGX in December 2014, was Asia's first pure-play data centre REIT and is managed by Keppel DC REIT Management Pte. Ltd., with Keppel Ltd (Keppel Capital) as sponsor. It owns a diversified portfolio of 25 data centres across 10 countries in Asia Pacific and Europe (assets under management of approximately S$6.3 billion as at end-2025), comprising a mix of fully-fitted colocation, single-tenant and shell-and-core assets plus select debt securities, and has pivoted its strategy toward hyperscale data centres to capture AI and cloud demand.

business_model.summary: Keppel DC REIT earns rental income by leasing data centre capacity to clients under a mix of master leases (single tenant, longer-dated, more fixed rent) and fully-fitted colocation arrangements (shorter contractual periods, higher variable/escalation-linked rent tied to power/space usage). Income is highly recurring (REIT structure, long WALE) but increasingly concentrated in a small number of very large hyperscale cloud/AI clients, and growth is driven by accretive acquisitions, positive rental reversions, and asset enhancement/redevelopment initiatives funded by a mix of debt and equity (including payment-in-units for management fees).
business_model.customer_type: B2B - hyperscale cloud service providers (AWS, Microsoft, Google, Alibaba, Tencent and similar), enterprises, financial institutions, telcos and government/regulated clients; hyperscalers now account for the majority of rental income
business_model.geographic_mix: Singapore ~68% of gross revenue (1H 2026), Japan ~9%, Ireland ~8%, Netherlands ~4%, China ~5%, Germany ~2%, other countries (Australia, UK, Italy, Malaysia) ~5%; by investment property value Singapore ~63%, Japan ~14%, Ireland ~6%, China ~4%, Netherlands ~4%, Germany ~3%, other ~6%

main_competitors: Mapletree Industrial Trust / Mapletree Pan Asia Commercial Trust
competitive_position.market_position: One of the largest pure-play data centre REITs in Asia Pacific and the only SGX-listed pure-play data centre REIT; a newly admitted Straits Times Index (STI) constituent (June 2025) reflecting its scale and visibility; owns full or majority stakes in several of Singapore's scarce, moratorium-protected data centre sites

moat_factors.factor: Scarce land/power access in supply-constrained hubs
moat_factors.description: Singapore's 2019-2022 data centre moratorium and ongoing land/power scarcity in markets such as Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Dublin and Tokyo make existing, powered sites highly defensible; Keppel DC REIT holds some of the few grandfathered Singapore DC sites with secured long-term land tenure (e.g., 10-year/30-year lease extensions secured for KDC SGP 1, 7 and 8)

Data centre migrations are costly, operationally risky and time-consuming for hyperscale/enterprise tenants once racks, power and connectivity are provisioned, supporting long WALE (6.7 years by lettable area) and high retention

Keppel Ltd provides deal sourcing, facility management capability (e.g., Keppel Data Centres) and integrated infrastructure/connectivity expertise, supporting a pipeline of related-party and third-party acquisitions

25 assets across 10 countries diversify geographic, regulatory and tenant risk relative to smaller single-market DC landlords, and scale supports access to capital markets (STI inclusion, green financing)
First-mover as Asia's pure-play DC REIT since 2014 with a 317% total unitholder return since listing and consistent DPU growth, aiding capital-raising credibility

weaknesses: Rising hyperscaler concentration (one client ~43.5% of 1H2026 rental income; hyperscalers ~69% of FY2025 rental income) creates significant counterparty and re-leasing risk

External manager structure (Keppel DC REIT Management) creates fee-based incentive misalignment risk — base and performance fees rose faster than DPU in some periods, and management fees are partly paid in units (dilutive)
Older, non-hyperscale assets (e.g., KDC SGP 1) face falling occupancy (46.5% reported) and may require costly redevelopment or repositioning
Smaller absolute scale than global giants Digital Realty and Equinix, limiting negotiating leverage with the largest hyperscale tenants
Reliance on third-party facility managers across multiple jurisdictions introduces operational execution risk

growth_drivers: AI and hyperscaler-driven demand: global colocation demand projected to grow faster than supply through 2029F, with AI inference workloads emerging as a key secular driver

Accretive M&A: $1.1 billion of acquisitions in 2025 (Tokyo Data Centre 3 hyperscale asset, remaining stakes in Keppel DC Singapore 3/4/7/8) funded partly via a $404.5 million preferential offering (168.2% subscribed)
Positive rental reversions: portfolio-wide reversion of approximately 45% in FY2025 and ~10% in 1H2026, reflecting mark-to-market upside as older/below-market leases roll

Redevelopment/asset enhancement pipeline: unlocking additional saleable power and converting unused space into new data halls at Keppel DC Singapore 8 (targeted completion 3Q2027); evaluating redevelopment of ageing Singapore asset KDC SGP 1
Capital recycling: divestments of non-core assets (Kelsterbach DC, Basis Bay DC, NetCo bonds) intended to redeploy ~$0.2 billion into higher-yielding hyperscale opportunities
Secured long-term land tenure (10-year and 30-year extensions for Keppel DC Singapore 1, 7 and 8) protects against moratorium-related land scarcity and locks in future redevelopment optionality
Structural data centre supply/demand imbalance in APAC and Europe, particularly constrained markets (Singapore, Tokyo, Dublin, Frankfurt), supporting continued rental growth

business.description: A single hyperscaler contributed 43.5% of 1H2026 rental income, and hyperscalers overall contributed 69.3% of FY2025 rental income (up from 61.1% in FY2024); loss, downsizing or renegotiation by a top client could materially impact income

Portfolio occupancy fell from 95.8% (FY2025) to 92.5% (1Q2026) partly due to the Cardiff Data Centre contract expiry; older assets like KDC SGP 1 show much lower occupancy (46.5%) and may need redevelopment capex

business.risk: Competition from larger global and local operators
business.description: Digital Realty, Equinix, AirTrunk, NEXTDC, GDS/DayOne and STT GDC/Nxera compete for the same hyperscale and enterprise tenants, potentially pressuring rents in markets with new supply coming online (e.g., Singapore's new 700MW Jurong Island park, second CFA tranche)
Reliance on third-party and related-party facility managers across 10 countries for uptime, security, and maintenance of mission-critical infrastructure

financial.risk: Rising finance costs on higher gearing
financial.description: Aggregate leverage rose from 31.5% (FY2024) to 35.3% (FY2025) following debt-funded acquisitions; a 100bps rate increase would cut interest coverage ratio from 6.9x to 5.1x as at 1H2026

Portfolio spans SGD, JPY, EUR, GBP, AUD, CNY and MYR; distributable income is hedged (71.2% of loans hedged, foreign-sourced distributions progressively hedged to June 2027) but residual FX translation volatility remains (FY2025/1H2026 showed meaningful currency translation swings in other comprehensive income)

financial.risk: Dilution from unit issuance and fee payments in units
financial.description: Preferential offering raised $404.5 million (expanding units in issue by ~10.5% in FY2025); manager base/performance fees are partly settled in units, adding incremental dilution each period

financial.risk: Doubtful receivables at Guangdong data centres
financial.description: Recurring loss allowances for doubtful receivables relating to China (Guangdong) assets flagged in both FY2025 and 1H2026 filings

regulatory.risk: Singapore data centre moratorium / land allocation policy
regulatory.description: Singapore paused new data centre approvals in 2019-2022; subsequent capacity is released only via IMDA Call for Application (CFA) tranches with strict PUE/sustainability requirements, constraining supply growth and concentrating risk/benefit in incumbents like Keppel DC REIT

EU AI Act, EU Energy Efficiency Directive, Singapore's Digital Infrastructure Act, and China's 2026 Cybersecurity Law Amendments raise compliance costs and operational requirements (e.g., mandatory PUE targets, renewable energy sourcing deadlines) across jurisdictions

regulatory.risk: Data sovereignty and cross-border data rules
regulatory.description: India's PDPA, UK's Critical National Infrastructure designation for data centres, and various national sovereign-cloud rules could affect tenant siting decisions and cross-border operations
NetCo bonds divestment was held up pending clearance from Singapore's Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) and was ultimately terminated in May 2026 when the buyer could not satisfy conditions

macro.description: As a REIT with 35%+ aggregate leverage, distributable income is sensitive to rate moves; US Federal Reserve held rates steady in June 2026 and signalled rates could stay elevated for longer, a headwind for refinancing costs and valuation yields
World Bank projected global growth to slow to 2.5% in 2026 from 2.9% in 2025; though data centre demand is viewed as structurally resilient, a broader slowdown could dampen enterprise/cloud capex

macro.risk: Power/grid constraints and input cost inflation
macro.description: Data centre construction costs rose 5.5% in 2025 (though decelerating); power availability has overtaken cost as the primary constraint on new AI-ready capacity in Frankfurt, Dublin, Tokyo and Sydney, raising both construction and retrofit costs

US tariffs on semiconductors, chips and related materials, plus export controls on advanced AI chips, could affect capex costs and timing of hyperscaler build-outs in some markets, though a May 2025 rescission of the US AI Diffusion Rule eased some restrictions

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global data centre demand has outpaced supply for five consecutive years; total colocation demand is projected to grow at ~17-19% CAGR through 2029F versus ~15-18% supply growth, driven by cloud adoption and accelerating AI training/inference workloads. APAC is expected to be one of the fastest-growing regions, with its AI market alone projected to grow from US$85.2bn (2025) to US$283.9bn (2030).
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low to moderate - data centres are viewed as a defensive, mission-critical real estate subsector with long leases and high switching costs, but capex cycles of hyperscaler tenants and interest-rate-driven cap rate movements introduce some cyclicality to valuations and acquisition appetite
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High - REIT structure with 35.3% aggregate leverage (FY2025) and $2.3-2.4 billion of gross borrowings; distributable income and unit valuations are both directly and indirectly (via cap rates) sensitive to rate moves, partially mitigated by 71.2% interest rate hedging
key_input_costs: Construction costs (especially liquid-cooling/AI-ready retrofits, 5-10% cost premium)
Land and development costs in constrained hubs (Singapore, Frankfurt, Tokyo)

recent_developments.event: 1H2026 results: gross revenue up 14.5% YoY to $242.0m, DPU up 11.3% YoY to 5.714 cents, driven by Tokyo DC 3 contribution and positive rental reversions; portfolio occupancy declined to 92.5% from 95.6% in 1Q2026 due to Cardiff Data Centre contract expiry
Terminated the planned sale of NetCo (M1 Network) bonds and preference shares after the buyer could not satisfy conditions precedent within the agreed timeline
Completed acquisition of remaining 10.0% interest in Keppel DC Singapore 3 and remaining 1.0% interest in Keppel DC Singapore 4, achieving full ownership of both assets
Paid $350 million lease extension consideration securing a 10-year land tenure extension for Keppel DC Singapore 7 and 8
Completed acquisition of a 98.47% effective interest in Tokyo Data Centre 3 (Inzai City, Greater Tokyo) for JPY 82.1 billion — the REIT's largest overseas acquisition since listing
Raised $404.5 million via preferential offering (168.2% subscribed) to fund Tokyo DC 3 and other growth initiatives; units in issue expanded ~10.5% for FY2025
Included in the FTSE Straits Times Index (STI) with effect from 23 June 2025, raising visibility among institutional and passive investors
Divested Kelsterbach Data Centre (Germany) at a premium to valuation and entered agreements to divest Basis Bay Data Centre (Malaysia), sharpening the portfolio toward hyperscale assets
Full-year distributable income rose 55.2% YoY to $268.1m and DPU rose 9.8% YoY to a record 10.381 cents; hyperscaler share of rental income rose to 69.3% from 61.1%

items.target: Continue pivot to hyperscale-focused portfolio via accretive acquisitions and capital recycling
items.notes: No explicit numeric AUM or DPU guidance disclosed (REIT does not provide formal point guidance); qualitative commentary emphasizes continued hyperscale/AI-focused growth and disciplined capital management

items.target: Maintain gearing with debt headroom for growth (35.3% at FY2025, 34.0% at 1H2026)
items.notes: Management cites ~$673m-$752m of unutilised debt facilities as at 1H2026 providing flexibility for further acquisitions

items.target: 71.2% of loans hedged; foreign-sourced distributions progressively hedged till end-June 2027
items.notes: Disciplined hedging strategy intended to protect capital and distribution stability amid elevated-for-longer rate environment

items.target: Complete Keppel DC Singapore 8 asset enhancement (additional data hall from unlocked saleable power)
items.notes: Separately evaluating potential redevelopment of ageing Keppel DC Singapore 1 given low (46.5%) occupancy

guidance.management_commentary: Management (CEO Loh Hwee Long, Chairman Christina Tan) highlighted sustained momentum from AI/cloud-driven demand, noted global macro uncertainty (US rates expected to stay elevated, geopolitical tensions, World Bank's 2.5% 2026 global growth forecast) as a backdrop risk, but emphasized the REIT's portfolio is 'well positioned to support cloud and AI inference workloads' and that the Manager remains focused on 'enhancing portfolio quality and maintaining financial flexibility to capture accretive growth opportunities.'

bull_case: Structural AI/cloud tailwind: global colocation demand is forecast to outpace supply through 2029, and Keppel DC REIT's portfolio sits in supply-constrained, high-barrier markets (Singapore, Tokyo, Dublin) well positioned to capture pricing power

Strong reversion and acquisition-led growth track record: ~45% portfolio rental reversion in FY2025 and 55% distributable income growth, funded by accretive, largely overseas (Tokyo DC3) and full-ownership (Singapore) acquisitions

Scarce, secured land positions: 10-year and 30-year land tenure extensions for key Singapore assets lock in long-term optionality in a moratorium-constrained market, a durable competitive moat versus new entrants
Index inclusion and institutional recognition (STI constituent since June 2025, 16 analysts covering, mostly Buy ratings) improves liquidity and lowers cost of capital for future growth
Prudent balance sheet with headroom: 35.3% aggregate leverage, 7.5x interest coverage (FY2025) and committed hedging provide flexibility to keep acquiring without over-levering
bear_case: Heavy and rising hyperscaler concentration (one client ~43.5% of 1H2026 rental income, hyperscalers ~69% of FY2025 rental income) creates outsized counterparty risk if a major cloud tenant renegotiates, consolidates, or leaves

Rate sensitivity: a 100bps rate rise would cut interest coverage from 6.9x to 5.1x, and distribution yield (~4.6-5.1%) competes directly with rising risk-free rates if the 'higher for longer' Fed stance persists

Occupancy softness and legacy-asset drag: portfolio occupancy fell from 95.8% to 92.5% within two quarters (Cardiff contract expiry), and older Singapore assets like KDC SGP1 (46.5% occupied) may require costly redevelopment
External manager fee structure (base + performance fees, partly paid in units) creates potential incentive misalignment and ongoing unit dilution as AUM grows

Multi-jurisdiction regulatory complexity (EU AI Act, Singapore's Digital Infrastructure Act, China's Cybersecurity Law Amendments) raises compliance costs and could slow or constrain future capacity additions across several of the REIT's markets
